target.title: Model risk management, including vendor and AI-based models (SR 26-2)

record.title: Model risk management, including vendor and AI-based models (SR 26-2)
record.statement: Issued by the Federal Reserve, OCC and FDIC on 17 April 2026, SR 26-2 'supersedes and replaces SR letter 11-7'. It defines a model as 'a complex quantitative method, system, or approach' that applies statistical, economic or financial theories to produce quantitative estimates. Its principles apply to 'non-generative, non-agentic AI models'; it treats generative and agentic AI as 'novel and rapidly evolving' and outside its scope. For vendor models it states that 'the principles of model risk management remain applicable': understand, validate and monitor them, and document customisations. It states that it 'does not set forth enforceable standards' and that non-compliance 'will not result in supervisory criticism'. It is most relevant to banking organisations with over $30 billion in total assets.

target.title: Third-party relationships: life cycle risk management, including AI providers (2023 interagency guidance)

record.title: Third-party relationships: life cycle risk management, including AI providers (2023 interagency guidance)
record.statement: The Federal Reserve, FDIC and OCC guidance 'is final as of June 6, 2023'. It describes risk management across the life cycle of a third-party relationship (planning, due diligence and selection, contract negotiation, ongoing monitoring, termination), states that 'the board has ultimate oversight responsibility', calls for contracts that generally include 'provisions for periodic, independent audits of the third party and its relevant subcontractors', and addresses how a bank evaluates its third party's own oversight of subcontractors. It does not mention AI; it reaches any arrangement under which an AI capability is provided to the bank. It remains in effect until replaced by the guidance proposed on 11 September 2026.

target.title: Proposed replacement of the 2023 third-party guidance (September 2026)

record.title: Proposed replacement of the 2023 third-party guidance (September 2026)
record.statement: On 11 September 2026 the OCC, Federal Reserve, FDIC and, for the first time on this subject, the NCUA proposed guidance 'revising and replacing existing guidance on third-party risk management'. The OCC bulletin states that 'non-compliance with the guidance will not result in supervisory action against a banking organization'. Commentary reports that the proposal replaces 'critical activities' with 'higher risk' relationships, organises practice into four risk management components, and states there are no generally applicable expected contract terms. The bulletin does not mention AI. Comments closed 16 November 2026.

target.title: New York: third-party service provider security policy, reaching AI providers (23 NYCRR 500.11)

record.title: New York: third-party service provider security policy, reaching AI providers (23 NYCRR 500.11)
record.statement: Section 500.11(a) provides that 'Each covered entity shall implement written policies and procedures designed to ensure the security of information systems' and nonpublic information held by third-party service providers, based on its risk assessment, addressing 'the identification and risk assessment of third-party service providers', minimum cybersecurity practices, due diligence, and 'periodic assessment of such third-party service providers based on the risk they present'. Section 500.11(b) addresses access controls, encryption, notice of cybersecurity events affecting the covered entity, and representations and warranties. The section applies in New York to DFS-licensed banks, insurers and other financial services companies, and reaches AI providers that hold or can reach their systems or data.

target.title: Written AI systems programme and oversight of third-party AI (NAIC model bulletin, as adopted by states)

record.title: Written AI systems programme and oversight of third-party AI (NAIC model bulletin, as adopted by states)
record.statement: Adopted by the NAIC on 4 December 2023 for states to issue as their own bulletins, it states that insurers 'are expected to develop, implement, and maintain a written program' for the responsible use of AI systems, with responsibility in 'senior management accountable to the board or an appropriate committee of the board'. For third-party AI systems and data it calls for due diligence and, where appropriate and available, contract terms that provide 'audit rights and/or entitle the Insurer to receive audit reports by qualified auditing entities' and that 'Require the third party to cooperate with the Insurer with regard to regulatory inquiries and investigations'. A programme may rely on frameworks such as 'the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework'. It applies in a state only once that state's insurance regulator issues it.

target.title: New York: AI and external data in underwriting and pricing, with vendor contract terms (Circular Letter 7)

record.title: New York: AI and external data in underwriting and pricing, with vendor contract terms (Circular Letter 7)
record.statement: Dated 11 July 2024, the letter addresses AI systems, external data and predictive models in 'underwriting and pricing insurance policies'. It states that 'The role of an insurer's board of directors, or other governing body, is to provide oversight of the insurer's activities' and that 'Senior management is responsible for day-to-day implementation'. Insurers 'retain responsibility for understanding any tools' used, and where appropriate and available should include contract terms that '(i) provide audit rights or entitle the insurer to receive audit reports by qualified auditing entities' and '(ii) require the third-party vendor to cooperate with the insurer regarding regulatory inquiries and investigations'.

target.title: Incident response and service provider oversight, with 72-hour breach notice (Regulation S-P)

record.title: Incident response and service provider oversight, with 72-hour breach notice (Regulation S-P)
record.statement: Rule 248.30(a)(3) calls for a response program 'reasonably designed to detect, respond to, and recover from unauthorized access' to customer information. Rule 248.30(a)(5) provides for written policies and procedures requiring oversight of service providers, through due diligence and monitoring, so that a service provider protects customer information and notifies the covered institution as soon as possible and no later than 72 hours after becoming aware of a breach affecting a customer information system it maintains. The institution may have a service provider give customer notices on its behalf but remains responsible for them. It reaches AI providers that receive, maintain or process customer information.

target.title: Supervisory system and written supervisory procedures, including over AI use (FINRA Rule 3110)

record.title: Supervisory system and written supervisory procedures, including over AI use (FINRA Rule 3110)
record.statement: Rule 3110(a) provides that 'Each member shall establish and maintain a system to supervise the activities of each associated person' reasonably designed to achieve compliance with securities laws and FINRA rules, and Rule 3110(b)(1) that each member 'shall establish, maintain, and enforce written procedures to supervise the types of business in which it engages'. The rule does not mention AI; FINRA treats its rules as technology-neutral, so a member's supervisory system and procedures reach its use of AI tools and agents.

record.title: Generative AI and AI agents: supervision, testing and monitoring (FINRA 2026 oversight report)
record.statement: Published 9 December 2025, the report has a standalone section on generative AI that reminds firms of their continuing obligations, describes expectations for governance, testing and monitoring, and for the first time addresses AI agents, which it describes as 'systems or programs that are capable of autonomously performing and completing tasks on behalf of a user'. target.title: Identify and mitigate discrimination risk in patient care decision support tools, including AI (45 CFR 92.210)

record.title: Identify and mitigate discrimination risk in patient care decision support tools, including AI (45 CFR 92.210)
record.statement: Section 92.210(a) provides that 'A covered entity must not discriminate on the basis of race, color, national origin, sex, age, or disability' through the use of patient care decision support tools. Section 92.210(b) sets 'an ongoing duty to make reasonable efforts to identify uses of patient care decision support tools' that employ input variables measuring those characteristics, and 92.210(c) to 'make reasonable efforts to mitigate the risk of discrimination resulting from the tool's use'. The defined tools include automated and non-automated tools, AI among them, used in clinical decision-making that affects patient care.

target.title: Business associate contracts for AI providers handling electronic health information (HIPAA Security Rule)

record.title: Business associate contracts for AI providers handling electronic health information (HIPAA Security Rule)
record.statement: Section 164.308(b) permits a covered entity to let a business associate create, receive, maintain or transmit electronic protected health information on its behalf only with satisfactory assurances, documented in a contract or other arrangement. Section 164.314(a)(2)(i) provides that the contract provide that the business associate will '(A) Comply with the applicable requirements of this subpart', '(B) ... ensure that any subcontractors that create, receive, maintain, or transmit electronic protected health information' agree to do the same, and '(C) Report to the covered entity any security incident of which it becomes aware'. An AI provider that processes electronic health information for a covered entity is reached as a business associate.

target.title: HTI-5 removes model-card and risk management criteria for decision support in certified health IT

record.title: HTI-5 removes model-card and risk management criteria for decision support in certified health IT
record.statement: Published on 28 October 2026 and effective 28 December 2026 for this change, HTI-5 narrows the decision support interventions certification criterion: certified health IT no longer has to support source attributes ('model cards') or apply intervention risk management to predictive decision support. The change binds certified health IT developers, not providers. For a hospital or health system it removes a federal baseline of information about predictive tools embedded in certified software; the provider's own duty under 45 CFR 92.210 is unchanged, so that information now has to be sought from the vendor by contract or due diligence.

target.title: Supply chain cyber security risk management plans for bulk electric system vendors, including AI tools (CIP-013-2)

record.title: Supply chain cyber security risk management plans for bulk electric system vendors, including AI tools (CIP-013-2)
record.statement: CIP-013-2 aims 'to mitigate cyber security risks to the reliable operation of the Bulk Electric System (BES)' by 'implementing security controls for supply chain risk management of BES Cyber Systems'. R1 provides that 'Each Responsible Entity shall develop one or more documented supply chain cyber security risk management plan(s)', including processes to identify and assess 'cyber security risk(s) to the Bulk Electric System from vendor products or services' and procurement processes addressing vendor incident notification, coordination of responses, access revocation, 'Disclosure by vendors of known vulnerabilities', software integrity and authenticity, and 'Coordination of controls for vendor-initiated remote access'. R3 calls for review and CIP Senior Manager approval 'at least once every 15 calendar months'. The standard does not mention AI; it reaches AI products and services procured for high and medium impact BES Cyber Systems.

target.title: Cyber incident (72 hours) and ransom payment (24 hours) reporting to CISA, from the final rule (CIRCIA)

record.title: Cyber incident (72 hours) and ransom payment (24 hours) reporting to CISA, from the final rule (CIRCIA)
record.statement: Section 681b(a)(1)(A) provides that a covered entity 'shall report the covered cyber incident to the Agency not later than 72 hours' after it reasonably believes the incident occurred, and 681b(a)(2)(A) that it 'shall report the payment to the Agency not later than 24 hours after the ransom payment has been made'. Under 681b(a)(7) these duties 'shall take effect on the dates prescribed in the final rule'. CISA sent its final rule to OIRA for review on 1 October 2026. Covered entities are to be defined by the rule across the critical infrastructure sectors. An incident in which an AI system or AI provider is the vector or the target is reached like any other.

target.title: California: automated decisionmaking technology and risk assessments (CCPA regulations)

record.title: California: automated decisionmaking technology and risk assessments (CCPA regulations)
record.statement: Section 7001(e) defines ADMT as 'any technology that processes personal information and uses computation to replace human decisionmaking or substantially replace human decisionmaking'. Section 7200(a) provides that 'A business that uses ADMT to make a significant decision concerning a consumer must comply' with Article 11 (notice, opt-out and access), and 7200(b) that a business already doing so 'must be in compliance with the requirements of this Article no later than January 1, 2027'. Section 7150(b)(3) lists 'Using ADMT for a significant decision concerning a consumer' among the processing that calls for a risk assessment before it begins; for processing begun before the regulations took effect, 7155(b) sets 31 December 2027.

target.title: Texas: prohibited AI uses, disclosure and Attorney General enforcement (TRAIGA)

record.title: Texas: prohibited AI uses, disclosure and Attorney General enforcement (TRAIGA)
record.statement: The Act 'takes effect January 1, 2026'. It prohibits developing or deploying AI with intent to manipulate behaviour towards self-harm, harm to others or crime, to infringe constitutional rights, or to unlawfully discriminate (disparate impact alone is not sufficient), and restricts government social scoring and biometric capture. Governmental agencies disclose AI interaction to consumers, and where AI is used in relation to health care services or treatment the disclosure is given 'not later than the date the service or treatment is first provided'. The Attorney General gives notice and a 60-day cure period before suit; a defendant is not liable where it finds a violation through internal review and 'substantially complies with the most recent version of the' NIST AI Risk Management Framework: Generative AI Profile or another recognised framework.

target.title: Colorado: notice, explanation and human review for automated decisions, from 2027 (SB 26-189)

record.title: Colorado: notice, explanation and human review for automated decisions, from 2027 (SB 26-189)
record.statement: Signed on 14 May 2026 and taking effect 1 January 2027, SB 26-189 replaces the 2024 Colorado AI Act's duty of care, risk management programmes and impact assessments with a narrower framework for automated decision-making technology that materially influences consequential decisions about consumers (education, employment, housing, financial services, insurance, health care and essential government services). Commentary reports that deployers give notice before use, a plain-language explanation after an adverse outcome, meaningful human review on request where commercially reasonable, and keep records for three years; developers give deployers documentation of intended uses, known harmful uses, limitations and human-review instructions. Contract terms purporting to indemnify a party for its own discriminatory acts are reported to be void. The Attorney General makes rules and gives a 60-day cure period until 2030.
